Old Folks

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We spend a day in Cape Town with older people who share their pensions to foster positive change and provide a glimmer of hope to the less fortunate.

Unique Selling Point:
Pensioners are often looked upon as forgotten, people no longer useful. But age is only a number and a positive mindset is all that is needed to create a better world for others. The real heroes are the ones who help others without expecting anything in return.

Summary:
The festive season is a time of joy and a time of sharing.g But for some it is a way of life. Four remarkable seniors use their state pension to bring hope to people in their community who are less fortunate.

Further information:
Daniel and Minnie Hoorn feed between 300 and 500 people in Capricorn, reputedly the oldest informal settlement in the Western Cape, and surrounding areas every week using their pensions plus small vegetable and bread donations. They have been doing this for 25 years. They are this year’s winners of the Community Champions Elders Awards.

For more than 20 years, since retiring from work at a filling station in Bergvliet, Cape Town, Daniel Hoorn had been feeding residents. He began the project with his first wife, Marie. “It is in my nature to help wherever I can. I didn’t understand, but I saw my father doing the same thing when I grew up. But then I gave my heart to the Lord and now I saw that giving was my calling.”

Minnie said she was known as a giving person so residents would knock on her door asking for food. “I could never understand that they always came to my door for a piece of bread, even when I was struggling, but I could always give them something and share. When Daniel’s wife passed on, Daniel came to my door and told me God told him to marry me,” Minnie says. Initially hesitant, she then realised they were meant to help the community as husband and wife.

The pair began providing meals for the hungry about 12 years ago. They do a mass feeding from the Help to Care Centre every Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday.

The soup kitchen started with their pensions; later, they began receiving donations from Woolworths and Pick n Pay. “But sometimes, we have nothing to give. I’ll be here saying: ‘Where are we going to get the food to feed?’ Something will always come through God’s grace. Daniel is a respected member of the community and he is often asks for spiritual advice.


93-year-old Mavis from Durbanville came from Zimbabwe when she was in her late 70s. She and her husband, Ferdinand, lived in the country for 46 years, but when the political situation became unbearable, they left with only a car and caravan, some clothing and three lampstands.

When her husband died in 2006, she felt an enormous sense of loss. They didn’t have any children, so Mavis decided to share the little she had. She took some of her pension money and, in her words, “put her hands to good use”.

At first, she knitted for people in disadvantaged communities such as Morningstar in Durbanville. For the past seven years, she has been putting her needles to good use for the Tygerbear Foundation at Tygerberg Hospital to bring a little sunshine to traumatised children and families.

Over the past 11 years, despite suffering from arthritis and osteoporosis, she has knitted more than 1 000 teddies and a few 1 000 beanies for charity – all with her state pension. She buys most of the wool herself, but welcomes any donations..

She also makes Christmas crackers for the Alta du Toit Centre, a home for adults with learning disabilities. She fills empty toilet rolls with sweets and wraps them in gift paper. She plans to make 200 crackers this year.

“The good Lord provides and finds work for idle hands. If I had to sit back and feel sorry for myself because I don’t have money to buy what I like, I would only have gotten into mischief,” she says.

Mavis has a great sense of humour. “When I wash my face in the morning and I see the funny face in the mirror, I laugh all day. I always say ‘I am a weed – flowers die; a weed only wilts’,” she says cheerfully.

Mavis still lives on her own and only depends on others to get to the shops. She has recently had a hip operation and, with the help of a walking ring, is still able to fix dinner and get around her garden to feed the birds.

Sheraaz Maarman, also known as the Muhammad Ali of South Africa because of his quick steps and fast punches in the ring, is 76 and lives in Bishop Lavis on the Cape Flats. Sheraaz started his boxing career in 1965 when he was only a youngster. At 19, he won the national lightweight crown and the Western Province light welterweight title. However, tragedy struck soon after when a car accident brought his boxing career to an end.

“I decided then that I would use my skills and knowledge to train others and have been doing so for the past 50 years,” he says.

“My aim is to give young people an alternative to drugs, gangsterism and other crime,” he says. He is currently training about 80 youngsters – half of them girls – at no cost. With no funds available for a premises and practice taking place on a field, training is restricted to the dry summer months.

“We want to have a clubhouse where we can train, but have been struggling to get the help we need. My dream is to have a place where young people can come together and learn a new skill and change their mindset, which will help them take charge of their lives,” he says.

“I use my own personal funds to support the young boxers. I have purchased gloves and some basic equipment, which is extremely costly, but I do it because boxing and all sports have a way of bringing people together, changing mindsets and lifting the stigma attached to our community. Our community is more than the drugs and gangsterism. We have many stories of success and we want to continue this through boxing,” he says.

Sheraaz hopes to see more doors open for young people in sport and for those doors to remain open for many years to come. He also runs a small soup kitchen out of his house.

Our story:
With Christmas around the corner, many people, old and young, are searching for meaning in their lives. We bring the story of the elderly who have become the givers and through their positive attitude have found a purpose for getting up every morning.

Script: Old folks give back
Duration: 8 minutes

V/O The Festive season is a time of joy and a time of sharing. But for some it is a way of life. Four remarkable seniors use their state pension to bring hope to the people in their communities.

Mavis Frew: I am 93; I can still touch my toes; I can do the dance of the seven veils but the trouble is you have to run away before I get to the seventh because I haven’t got a very pretty figure.

V/O Mavis Frew lives in a rambling house in Durbanville, a northern suburb of Cape Town, where she is a boarder. Her daily routine is mapped out. She makes a cup of black tea for herself and talks to the dogs. Then she settles down in her favourite chair with her knitting and her mind wanders to the early years when Zimbabwe was still Rhodesia.

Mavis Frew: When I was working I was a private secretary. I have a few brains, not many.

Claire Mawisa: And then where did you learn how to knit?

Mavis Frew: I started knitting teddy bears when I was in northern Rhodesia and I made them all for the abused children. They said you know Mavis it is a wonderful gift you are giving to those children. They cling to those teddy bears. And that made me feel nice.

V/O After 47 years, Mavis and her late husband left Zimbabwe and settled in Cape Town. She continued knitting beanies and teddy bears for disadvantaged children in her community - even now funding suppplies from her state pension.
LINK: Over the years Mavis has knitted thousands of these adorable teddy bears that she insists gets handed out to abused children. In Cape Town they go to the Tygerbear Foundation for traumatised children and families.
Up sound - children playing with the knitted teddies

Claire Mawisa: You also make crackers?

Mavis Frew: Yes I make Christmas crackers.

Claire Mawisa: Who gets your crackers?

Mavis Frew: I give them to the Alta du Toit old people’s home. I give them 220 this year and then the Alta du Toit children’s home also to them.

V/O Despite a recent hip operation, which means she needs a walker to get around, for Mavis, age is just a number and Bingo is her game.

Up sound - bingo game

Mavis Frew: Always think that someone is off worse than you. Like if I am feeling sad, then I suddenly think there is somebody worse off than me. There always is.

V/O With these words of wisdom we left for Vrygrond, the oldest informal settlement in the Western Cape where unemployment affects almost every family. Many depend on handouts.
Link: I am in Vrygrond in Cape Town where Daniel and Minnie Hoorn run a soup kitchen where they feed three to five-hundred members of the community three times a week and the soup kitchen has been running for thirteen years.
Up sound - prayer (Our Father who art in heaven).

Daniel Hoorn: Ek het opgegroei met dit om te kan help. (I grew up with the purpose of helping) Daar het ek gesien by the huis as n kind (At home I saw as a child) hoe my oupa mense help (how my grandfather helped people) wat nie agter gekyk word nie. (who were not looked after.)

V/O Eighty-one-year old Daniel started a small soup kitchen twenty-five-years ago. Then he was married to Marie. When she passed away, Daniel asked Minnie, now 71, to marry him.

Minnie Hoorn: When Daniel came to me and said to me God send me to you because your spiritual life is going a little bit down. And I said me, I don’t want to get married but anyhow he said I will come back in a week’s time. You can think about it.

Claire Mawisa: And Daniel did she think about it. What happened?

Minnie Hoorn: We are eleven years married now.

Up sound - kitchen

V/O Together, they took on the big responsibility of feeding the hundreds of people of Vrygrond - using their state pensions plus small donations from grocery stores.

Minie Hoorn: Daar is baie tye dat ek gewonder het hoe gaan ek dit maak (There have been times that I wondered how we are going to manage) want ons nou begin om die kos uit te gee (because when we start to dish out the food) dan is daar so baie, die hele straat is so vol mense. (then there are so many; the street is full of people.) Ek wil vir jou se dan kom die Here vir ons deur. (I want to tell you, then God comes to our aid).

V/O For Minnie and Daniel, bringing a little hope to those who have given up on life is their way of life.

Daniel Hoorn: Hulle het nie kos in die huis nie; (They don’t have food in the house;) hulle het nie klere nie; (they don’t have clothes;) dan help ek maar in my swakheid. (then I help in my weakness.)

Minnie Hoorn: Ons het nooit eendag beskaamd gestaan nie… (We have never, one day, been let down.) nooit nie…want die Here het elke dag voorsien. (...never…God always provided.)

V/O Making something out of nothing, is 76-year-old Sheraaz Maarman’s speciality. Known as Cape Town’s Mohammed Ali in the nineteen-sixties, boxing caught his fascination at a young age and he joined a club in Seapoint.

Sheraaz Maarman: There was a small boxing club, all the people working for the docks. The boys come there and starting. “Left and right, uppercut. Left and right, uppercut.” And I say: “Ay I duck and I am waving”. They say: “No it is good. You can come and box here one day.”

V/O By the age of 18 Sheraaz was amateur lightweight champion and the Western Province light-welterweight title holder. A car accident in his twenties meant giving up what he loved most.

Sheraaz Maarman: I got an accident on the mountain, the car rolling with us and the doctor said I must stop boxing.

V/O But drawing on his passion, Sheraaz started up a boxing club in Bishop Lavis where he trained several South African champions in various weight divisions.

Up sound

V/O Over the years, funds ran out and the formal boxing club closed down, but Sheraaz has never given up on the sport and on getting children off the streets and away from drugs and gangsters.

Claire: Explain the current situation in Bishop Lavis?

Sheraaz Maarman: The father is out of work. Lots of people haven’t got work here. And I see the youngsters walking in the street and I say: “come man, let me try to box. Put on the gloves. Throw away that knife.”

Link: Without funds available for a clubhouse, training has to happen out in the open which means during the winter rainy months, everything grinds to a halt.

V/O Sheraaz has appealed to the City of Cape Town for a proper sports facility where he can train aspiring boxers. In the meantime, despite having no ring, just a few boxing gloves and little equipment, Sheraaz trains hundreds of boys and girls of various ages, every week.

Up sound - children boxing

Sheraaz Maarman: I said always: “your child is my child”. And I will look everybody, it doesn’t matter whose child it is. It is my child.

V/O Pensioners are often forgotten or ignored. But with unfaltering commitment and positive mindsets, these exceptional South Africans do what they can to create a better world for others.

Minnie Hoorn: They come for love they come for help. So you must give the people what they need. So that is my love what I know.

Claire Mawisa: How does it feel to know you have touched so many people’s lives with what you have been able to make with your hands?

Mavis Frew: I have never thought of it that way, funnily enough. So I do not think I am wonderful. I am just a normal person.

Claire Mawisa: What would your Christmas message be?

Mavis Frew: Help other people if you can. Never knock anybody down though. Rather pick them up if they are down. That is my message.

END

Claire: Explain the current situation in Bishop Lavis? Sheraaz Maarman: The father is out of work. Lots of people haven’t got work here. And I see the youngsters walking in the street and I say: “come man, let me try to box. Put on the gloves. Throw away that knife.” Link: Without funds available for a clubhouse, training has to happen out in the open which means during the winter rainy months, everything grinds to a halt. V/O Sheraaz has appealed to the City of Cape Town for a proper sports facility where he can train aspiring boxers. In the meantime, despite having no ring, just a few boxing gloves and little equipment, Sheraaz trains hundreds of boys and girls of various ages, every week. Up sound - children boxing Sheraaz Maarman: I said always: “your child is my child”. And I will look everybody, it doesn’t matter whose child it is. It is my child. V/O Pensioners are often forgotten or ignored. But with unfaltering commitment and positive mindsets, these exceptional South Africans do what they can to create a better world for others. Minnie Hoorn: They come for love they come for help. So you must give the people what they need. So that is my love what I know. Claire Mawisa: How does it feel to know you have touched so many people’s lives with what you have been able to make with your hands? Mavis Frew: I have never thought of it that way, funnily enough. So I do not think I am wonderful. I am just a normal person. Claire Mawisa: What would your Christmas message be? Mavis Frew: Help other people if you can. Never knock anybody down though. Rather pick them up if they are down. That is my message. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We spend a day in Cape Town with older people who share their pensions to foster positive change and provide a glimmer of hope to the less fortunate.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Pensioners are often looked upon as forgotten, people no longer useful. But age is only a number and a positive mindset is all that is needed to create a better world for others. The real heroes are the ones who help others without expecting anything in return.
metadata.Summary: The festive season is a time of joy and a time of sharing.g But for some it is a way of life. Four remarkable seniors use their state pension to bring hope to people in their community who are less fortunate.
metadata.Further information: Daniel and Minnie Hoorn feed between 300 and 500 people in Capricorn, reputedly the oldest informal settlement in the Western Cape, and surrounding areas every week using their pensions plus small vegetable and bread donations. They have been doing this for 25 years. They are this year’s winners of the Community Champions Elders Awards. For more than 20 years, since retiring from work at a filling station in Bergvliet, Cape Town, Daniel Hoorn had been feeding residents. He began the project with his first wife, Marie. “It is in my nature to help wherever I can. I didn’t understand, but I saw my father doing the same thing when I grew up. But then I gave my heart to the Lord and now I saw that giving was my calling.” Minnie said she was known as a giving person so residents would knock on her door asking for food. “I could never understand that they always came to my door for a piece of bread, even when I was struggling, but I could always give them something and share. When Daniel’s wife passed on, Daniel came to my door and told me God told him to marry me,” Minnie says. Initially hesitant, she then realised they were meant to help the community as husband and wife. The pair began providing meals for the hungry about 12 years ago. They do a mass feeding from the Help to Care Centre every Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday. The soup kitchen started with their pensions; later, they began receiving donations from Woolworths and Pick n Pay. “But sometimes, we have nothing to give. I’ll be here saying: ‘Where are we going to get the food to feed?’ Something will always come through God’s grace. Daniel is a respected member of the community and he is often asks for spiritual advice. 93-year-old Mavis from Durbanville came from Zimbabwe when she was in her late 70s. She and her husband, Ferdinand, lived in the country for 46 years, but when the political situation became unbearable, they left with only a car and caravan, some clothing and three lampstands. When her husband died in 2006, she felt an enormous sense of loss. They didn’t have any children, so Mavis decided to share the little she had. She took some of her pension money and, in her words, “put her hands to good use”. At first, she knitted for people in disadvantaged communities such as Morningstar in Durbanville. For the past seven years, she has been putting her needles to good use for the Tygerbear Foundation at Tygerberg Hospital to bring a little sunshine to traumatised children and families. Over the past 11 years, despite suffering from arthritis and osteoporosis, she has knitted more than 1 000 teddies and a few 1 000 beanies for charity – all with her state pension. She buys most of the wool herself, but welcomes any donations.. She also makes Christmas crackers for the Alta du Toit Centre, a home for adults with learning disabilities. She fills empty toilet rolls with sweets and wraps them in gift paper. She plans to make 200 crackers this year. “The good Lord provides and finds work for idle hands. If I had to sit back and feel sorry for myself because I don’t have money to buy what I like, I would only have gotten into mischief,” she says. Mavis has a great sense of humour. “When I wash my face in the morning and I see the funny face in the mirror, I laugh all day. I always say ‘I am a weed – flowers die; a weed only wilts’,” she says cheerfully. Mavis still lives on her own and only depends on others to get to the shops. She has recently had a hip operation and, with the help of a walking ring, is still able to fix dinner and get around her garden to feed the birds. Sheraaz Maarman, also known as the Muhammad Ali of South Africa because of his quick steps and fast punches in the ring, is 76 and lives in Bishop Lavis on the Cape Flats. Sheraaz started his boxing career in 1965 when he was only a youngster. At 19, he won the national lightweight crown and the Western Province light welterweight title. However, tragedy struck soon after when a car accident brought his boxing career to an end. “I decided then that I would use my skills and knowledge to train others and have been doing so for the past 50 years,” he says. “My aim is to give young people an alternative to drugs, gangsterism and other crime,” he says. He is currently training about 80 youngsters – half of them girls – at no cost. With no funds available for a premises and practice taking place on a field, training is restricted to the dry summer months. “We want to have a clubhouse where we can train, but have been struggling to get the help we need. My dream is to have a place where young people can come together and learn a new skill and change their mindset, which will help them take charge of their lives,” he says. “I use my own personal funds to support the young boxers. I have purchased gloves and some basic equipment, which is extremely costly, but I do it because boxing and all sports have a way of bringing people together, changing mindsets and lifting the stigma attached to our community. Our community is more than the drugs and gangsterism. We have many stories of success and we want to continue this through boxing,” he says. Sheraaz hopes to see more doors open for young people in sport and for those doors to remain open for many years to come. He also runs a small soup kitchen out of his house. Our story: With Christmas around the corner, many people, old and young, are searching for meaning in their lives. We bring the story of the elderly who have become the givers and through their positive attitude have found a purpose for getting up every morning.
